newsitem.title: HONG KONG: YEARENDER - Asia trade fears China soybean import cap.
newsitem.headline: YEARENDER - Asia trade fears China soybean import cap.

text.p: China imported a massive amount of soybeans and soymeal in 1996, but grains and oilseeds traders in Asia fear their business might shrivel in 1997 if Beijing slaps on import restrictions as expected.
Theories on why Beijing would take such a step despite China's growing need for soybeans, cover a wide spectrum.
"Imports of soybean and meal (in 1996) have gone up quite significantly -- one never knows whether this is a long-term kind of change in policy," said a senior U.S. industry source based in China.
"And if there are any kinds of restrictions put on, you wonder whether it's kind of a U-turn," he added.

Market talk that Beijing could impose limits on soybean imports in 1997 has swirled amongst Asian traders over the past few months, making Chinese buyers jittery about accepting cargoes that would arrive at China's ports after January 1.
Chinese enquiries for soybeans have slowed to a trickle in the latter weeks of 1996 on trade fears that this year's soybean import bonanza might be an isolated event.
"Almost for certain, there will be quotas, probably for about one million tonnes in 1997," said one China-based trader, echoing the market's anxiety.
Beijing has denied that it plans to limit soybean imports.

According to official figures, China imported 690,000 tonnes of soybeans in January to October this year, up 363 percent from the same period last year. Traders estimate soybean arrivals in 1996 will total from 900,000 tonnes to over one million tonnes.

The country's growing need for animal feed to fuel rising pork, beef and poultry consumption, combined with declining soybean acreage, point solidly to China needing more soybeans than it can produce in 1997, oilseeds traders said.
But they also had theories on why China could move to curb imports.
China has delayed until January 10 a plan to ban imports of some U.S. goods, including unspecified agricultural commodities, in retaliation for American import restrictions on Chinese textiles.

"Obviously, the imposition of this ill-defined (soybean import restriction) threat is itself a negotiation ploy and pressure tactic," the senior industry source said, noting that China was a valuable market for U.S. soybeans.
But other traders said all soybean imports, not just U.S. origin, could be at stake and sheltering Chinese farmers' profits was China's main impetus for restricting soybean imports.
"Limiting imports would protect the domestic market and the peasants' profits. I don't think it has anything to do with trade disputes," said a Beijing-based grains trader.
"If China casually imports (soybeans) like this year, then domestic prices will drop and peasants will be unwilling to plant," he said.
The trader noted oilseeds prices in China had already softened with soybeans dropping as much as 10 percent from the beginning of the year to around 3,300 yuan ($397) per tonne currently.
Some market players noted that limiting imports could drive up domestic prices and nudge inflation higher.
"I think stopping imports is not good for China. It would drive up inflation, so you're not protecting the farmers," a senior Hong Kong-based trader said.
Another trader argued that clamping down on speculation was the main reason behind a possible decision to restrict soybean imports.

"If China doesn't put a cap on imports, then a lot of people might go out and buy and speculate, because they know there is no limit, so they buy half a million tonnes and just wait, wait for the right time," he said.
Traders see a mediocre tally for China's soybean production this year, at about 13.3 million tonnes in the 1996 crop year (October to September), down 1.5 percent from last year.
Industry sources also estimate China's hog production -- which accounts for about 70 percent of China's meat consumption -- to grow at about 10 percent in 1997 to 500 million heads.
